name: Lena Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play the second bassoon part with a neighbourhood orchestra, record slow practice lines and teach two beginners. I started being paid for music in my fifties after shop work, finished secondary school and still ask the principal bassoonist to check my faster passages. I like the low note that holds the woodwinds together.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do the workdays fit the household now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner cooks at a school on regular hours and our children are grown. We rent a flat and have four months of expenses saved. The music pays about what this junior job usually does, and there are some similar posts nearby, though I cannot assume they have vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that a quicker booking email is useful when the paid rehearsal fee is still written beside it. The bassoonist still has to listen for the conductor’s breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our four months saved and my partner’s regular school wage make one delayed concert fee manageable. I still need the current orchestra contract because I have not checked what retirement will actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid orchestra calls, two beginner pupils and practice recordings this season. I have never used an AI tool and would check the printed schedule; before next season I would ask for a written cancellation fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this small change. The household can manage one late payment without borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a concert move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall closed for a heating repair last winter and paid the rehearsal, not the concert. A written half-fee term would make that less of a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help with a fee gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I would ask for a ride to a paid audition, not their rent money.

think: Our **four-month reserve** and partner wage cover one delayed concert fee.
My **retirement income** still needs checking before I stop working.
do: Keep **paid orchestra calls**, two pupils and recordings this season.
Request a **written half-fee term** before the next concert season.
feel: I feel **calm** because current work and savings cover one routine delay.
S0.quote: The bassoonist still has to listen for the conductor’s breath.
fieldNote: Her **late junior role** earns typical musician pay while she still learns from the principal player.

steps.text: Keep paid orchestra calls, two pupils and recordings this season
Request written half-fee cancellation term before next concert season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra manager that cheap generated practice parts could reduce my little recording fees. I would ask for a written paid rehearsal calendar before making other plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The slow bassoon lines bring about a quarter of my own pay. If orders fall, four months saved buys time, but it is not a replacement wage until retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would count the practice-line invoices and request signed paid dates. In the first year, if recording orders fall, I would stop hiring the separate practice room on unused days and keep my two pupils while asking a nearby ensemble about an advertised paid bassoon seat I can play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing a regular part of my earnings. I would rather know the actual paid dates than buy a tool I do not understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn an AI music app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used one and do not want to upload a pupil’s playing. I would watch a trusted teacher show it before making any decision, but I am not buying a trial licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any nearby seat do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would apply only if a seat is posted, the excerpts are within my ability, written net pay after travel beats the lost recording fees and the bus gets me home.

I would warn that **generated practice parts** threaten recording fees.

feel: I feel **anxious** about my own recording income shrinking.
S1.quote: I would rather know the actual paid dates than buy a tool I do not understand.
fieldNote: She stays **AI resistant** and makes no new tool-learning claim from watching a demonstration.
A different **bassoon seat** needs a real paid posting, playable excerpts, written net improvement and bus travel.

steps.text: Keep two beginner pupils while requesting signed paid orchestra dates
Stop separate practice-room hire on unused days if recording orders fall
Apply for posted playable seat if orders fall, after-travel net beats losses, bus fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that thinking AGI by 2028 could make our slow practice lines cheaply. Robots able to play the bassoon arrive around 2031, three years later, but the recording invoice can go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the practice-line orders to end in 2028, taking a quarter of my music pay. Some concert dates might also shrink; I cannot count a nearby job as mine until it is posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask for a signed paid orchestra calendar and total recording invoices. In the first year after 2028, if paid concerts fall too, I would apply for a posted music-library desk role only if my secondary schooling and shop experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus route fits; I would keep orchestra calls and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing the recordings. Four months of savings and a few local employers give us a search window, but I would be alarmed if concert pay collapsed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 60 instead of applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months saved is useful, but it does not cover years without work. I would keep paid bassoon work until a real pension statement shows we can afford to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a desk qualification first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read an actual posted job description. I would not spend savings on a course for a vacancy that might accept my shop experience.

Seek **posted library work** after 2028 concert cuts if secondary schooling/shop experience qualify, after-travel net replaces losses and bus fits.
Keep **orchestra and pupils** until a suitable written offer is signed.

S2.quote: I would keep paid bassoon work until a real pension statement shows we can afford to stop.
fieldNote: The **2028 recording loss** precedes 2031 playing robots, while concert cuts are uncertain.
A desk move needs **posted eligibility**, written net replacement pay, workable bus route and signed offer.

steps.text: Total recording invoices and request signed paid orchestra calendar now
Seek posted library role after 2028 concert cuts if secondary schooling/shop experience qualify and bus fits
Require written net after travel replacing losses; keep paid calls/pupils until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the music centre that five years until AGI by 2031 lets us see whether beginners will pay for a small woodwind group. Playing robots follow around 2034, after practice software changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recordings may end by 2031. A separate beginner bassoon circle could replace some fees if families pay for preparation, but an empty hall would cost more than it earns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would secure written room and hire terms from a separate community hall before taking fees. I would offer a four-week beginner bassoon circle only if five adults prepay enough for room hire, my teaching and preparation, with safe inspected loan instruments or their own sound bassoons. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat it only while five paid places still cover those costs, written room terms hold and instruments stay safe; I would keep my two regular pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the circle covers my time. Five years until AGI gives me one chance to test a paid bassoon class without paying hall rent from savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks a loan bassoon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre technician must check the joints and keys before an adult plays a loan bassoon. If one is unsafe, the adult needs a sound replacement instrument or another paying adult must take the place; below five fees I would defer and refund the circle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if just three adults prepay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three fees do not cover room hire or preparation. I would refund all three and keep teaching the two pupils I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to check what retirement actually pays. Playing robots arrive around 2039, but I cannot treat a birthday as a final pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need orchestra and pupil income. Four months saved is useful, yet I have not checked whether any pension would cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request my pension statement and save twenty percent of each extra paid concert fee after rent, food and instrument repairs until we have six months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid calls and pupils while the contracts hold, and seek a posted music-library desk job only if concert pay falls, my schooling and experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and the bus works; I would leave only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about work at 68, with current dates paying and some savings. I would not claim retirement is funded until I have the statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra concerts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then there is no twenty percent to save from that source. I would not cut food to make the reserve line look better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop playing at 68 if the statement is small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid work that I can do. I need real income numbers before deciding how much to slow down.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because practice-line pay could stop before I know if another orchestra or desk post is open. Signed concert dates, an actual pension statement and a posted job with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a junior player can still be learning at 58. I do scales each morning, and the rent still asks for a finished performance fee.

headlineQuote: I do scales each morning, and the rent still asks for a finished performance fee.
portrait: At **58**, Lena is a junior bassoonist with secondary schooling, a partner, grown children and four months saved.
Her **typical musician pay** comes from orchestra calls, two pupils and simple practice recordings, with some local openings.
She has **never used AI** and checks paid dates on paper while learning from the principal player.
She tests a **paid beginner circle** only with five prepayments covering room, her time and safe instruments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end practice-line pay before a real posted replacement role appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed concert dates**, a real pension statement and a posted job with written net replacement pay would help Lena.
